paragraphs.text: Lesson 11, why aren't you on time?
Listen to this conversation between Nate and Brad, two co-workers.
Do your best to answer the comprehension questions as you listen, then learn the expressions.
You're late again. This is the fourth time this week.
You've got to get your act together, or else you're going to be in hot water.
I overslept, okay? Why do you always got to get on my case?
It's not my fault that I'm tired all the time.
I'm working a second job, so I've been burning the midnight oil.
You have to work a second job because you rear-ended a BMW while speeding to work.
Why were you speeding? Could it be because you were running late?
The BMW cut in front of me and then slammed on the brakes,
and my insurance won't cover the entire repair bill.
I have to cough up 50% out of my own pocket.
Man, I'll be working a second job for the rest of my life.
Brad, things like this wouldn't happen to you if you only would get to work on time.
Take me, for example. I'm always right here at my desk at the stroke of nine.
Don't rub it in, Mr. Perfect.
It's not rocket science. All I do is set my alarm clock for 7 a.m.
So I've got plenty of time to take a shower, have a leisurely breakfast, read the paper,
and get to work without driving like a maniac.
Yeah, well, I set my alarm for 7, too. It's just that I hit the snooze button a couple of times.
Plus I've got a life. I've got a girlfriend who likes to go out. You know, I'm busy.
So I usually hit the sack around 2 a.m.
Hey, you don't need to explain yourself to me. But make sure the head honcho doesn't see you sneaking in at quarter to ten.
Overheard him tell the HR director that if you were late one more time this week, he'd give you the boot.
Wait, he said he would fire me? No way. Okay, granted I'm late a lot, but I make up for it during the day.
I get way more done than those slackers in the marketing department.
That may be true, but if you can't even manage to show up on time, how can the company count on you for anything that's remotely important?
If you get fired, then you brought it on yourself.
I can't afford to lose my job. I was planning on retiring with this company.
Well, you're in luck because the boss called in sick today. No one knows you arrived late except me.
But I can't cover for you all the time, so just make sure you're here by 9 from now on.
Thanks Nate. You're a lifesaver. I swear I'll be on time from now on.
No, I'll do better than that. I'll be early. Just wait and see. I'll get here earlier than you.
That's what I like to hear. Now, let's get to work.
Okay, let's learn the vocabulary from their conversation.
Nate tells Brad, you've got to get your act together or else you're going to be in hot water.
We have two idioms in that sentence. Get your act together means become better organized.
And in hot water means in trouble. So, Nate is saying you need to become better organized.
Or else you're going to be in trouble. Brad responds, I overslept okay. Why do you always got to get on my case?
To get on someone's case means to criticize that person in an annoying way.
Brad's excuse is that he's been working a second job, so he's been burning the midnight oil.
This expression, burning the midnight oil means to stay up late working or studying.
Nate points out that Brad has to work a second job because he rear-ended a BMW while speeding to work.
Rear-ended means hit the back of another car. And speeding means driving faster than the speed limit.
Why was Brad speeding? Because he was running late.
But Brad says it was the other driver's fault. He says the BMW cut in front of me and then slammed on the brakes.
This expression, slammed on the brakes, means stopped very suddenly.
The brakes are the equipment inside the car which will slow the car down or stop the car.
And Brad's insurance won't cover the entire repair bill. Brad says I have to cough up 50% out of my own pocket.
This phrasal verb cough up is used for giving money that you don't want to give.
So Brad has to pay 50% of the repair bill out of his own pocket. That means out of his own personal money.
Nate tells Brad that he should really get to work on time.
Nate says, take me for an example. I'm always right here at my desk at the stroke of nine.
At the stroke of nine means at exactly nine o'clock.
And Brad replies, don't rub it in, Mr. Perfect.
Rub it in means to keep talking about something that makes a person embarrassed or upset.
So Brad is telling Nate, don't keep talking about this topic because it's making me even more annoyed.
Nate explains it's not rocket science. This expression, it's not rocket science, means it's not difficult or complicated.
Nate sets his alarm clock for 7 a.m. So he has plenty of time to take a shower and have a leisurely breakfast.
Leisurely means slow and relaxed. And he can get to work without driving like a maniac. A maniac is a crazy person.
Brad says that he sets his alarm for 7 o'clock too. It's just that he hits the snooze button a couple of times.
Hit the snooze button means to delay the alarm for 8 to 10 minutes. And Brad does this a couple of times, so he wakes up later than 7 o'clock.
Brad likes to go out with his girlfriend and do a lot of other things, so he usually hits the sack around 2 a.m.
This expression, hit the sack, is a slang way to say go to bed. Another expression is hit the hay.
Both hit the hay and hit the sack mean go to bed.
Nate says, Hey, you don't need to explain yourself to me, but make sure the head honcho doesn't see you sneaking in at quarter to ten.
This expression, head honcho, is a slang word for the boss, the leader, or the person in charge.
Nate says, I overheard him tell the HR director that if you were late one more time this week, he'd give you the boot.
This verb overheard means to hear a conversation with someone else. You listen to somebody else's conversation, usually by accident.
The phrase give you the boot is an informal way to say fire you, terminate your employment. In other words, put you out of the company.
Brad can't believe it. He says, Okay, granted, I'm late a lot.
Granted means I acknowledge that this is true.
But, Brad says, I make up for it during the day.
Make up for it means compensate for it. Do something good to counterbalance or compensate the bad thing.
Brad says, I get way more done than those slackers in the marketing department.
Slackers is a slang word for lazy people, people who don't do their work.
Nate says that may be true, but if you can't even manage to show up on time, how can the company count on you?
The phrasal verb show up means arrive or appear, and the phrasal verb count on means depend on.
Nate warns Brad, if you get fired then you brought it on yourself.
You brought it on yourself means you caused your own problems.
Fortunately, the boss called in sick today, and Nate is the only one who knows that Brad arrived late.
But, Nate says, I can't cover for you all the time.
Cover for you means provide an excuse to help someone escape trouble.
So, Nate says, just make sure you're here by nine from now on.
From now on means from this moment and in the future.
Brad is very grateful. He says, thanks Nate, you're a lifesaver.
You're a lifesaver means you help me greatly when I need help.
Then Brad says, I swear I'll be on time from now on.
I swear means I promise very strongly.
In fact, Brad promises to get to work early.
And Nate says that's what I like to hear.
Hopefully, Brad will get his act together so that he doesn't get fired.
That's all the vocabulary from today's conversation.

and the speaking task to get some feedback on your spoken English.
